title: Use LongSupplier in AllocationService for nano time

timeline.message:
Use ThreadPool in AllocationService for nano time

AllocationService#currentNanoTime is relying on System.nanoTime().
Instead we should inject time using ThreadPool#relativeTimeInNanos

timeline.body:
AllocationService#currentNanoTime is relying on System.nanoTime(). Instead we should inject time using ThreadPool#relativeTimeInNanos

This is quite large PR. Navigate through the change in this order:
1. AllocationService takes ThreadPool as ctor param
2. ClusterModule injects ThreadPool into AllocationService
3. ESAllocationTestCase defines managed (setup/teardown) test thread pool which is used in test subclasses
4. DeterministicTaskQueue now uses System#currentTimeMillis as a time basis (used to be 0) 
5. Tune many tests which use AllocationService

Closes #89382

timeline.author: Volodymyr Krasnikov

timeline.body:
I don't follow why we need this change here. Really `currentTimeMillis` is a _relative_ time, so its absolute value shouldn't matter. I'm +1 on making it not start from zero, in fact I've wanted to do that for a while, but I'd rather it started from a random value (derived from the test seed) rather than the absolute current time since this is not repeatable.

Also I suggest breaking this change out into a separate PR. I expect that it _should_ be independent of this one, at least if it isn't then that suggests we have a bug somewhere.

reply.body: Restored original logic for DeterministicTaskQueue to use 0 as a time basis for task execution. In initial version of PR the time basis was changed to deal with timing issue in SnapshotResiliencyTests#testSnapshotPrimaryRelocations. Root cause is described in #95800. Whilst #95800 is not implemented to fix the test, custom timing adjustment is done, see changes to SnapshotResiliencyTests around L1619

timeline.body: This is a pretty heavy dependency - setting up and tearing down a whole `ThreadPool` for each test is too expensive for my liking. Could we pass in a `LongSupplier` instead, injecting `threadPool::relativeTimeInNanos` only where necessary? The only unit tests that care about time should be the ones that use a `MockAllocationService` for which we can pass in `() -> nanoTimeOverride`, and the others can just use `() -> 0L`.

reply.body:
Re `LongSupplier`. I wonder if it is better to introduce dedicated interface for this, similar to java.time.InstantSource or java.time.Clock with dedicated methods to retrieve time? (relativeTimeInMillis/relativeTimeInNanos/rawRelativeTimeInMillis/absoluteTimeInMillis).

Having dedicated interface would:
* make it clear what kind of time is actually used
* make it easier to have a simple test implementation 
* be easy to integrate with real implementation from ThreadPool

Sure, we could do that too. I'm not convinced we want `absoluteTimeInMillis` in there - the places that care about absolute time are rather different from the ones that care about relative time. Also not sure how big a change that would be, we use `LongSupplier` quite a bit already today.

> Also not sure how big a change that would be

May be it is worth a separate pr with general time injection improvements if that is too big.

> LongSupplier quite a bit already today.

I am not sure this is good in general as does not make it obvious if that is millis or nanos nor if it is cached or raw.
However I do not mind using that if above turns out to be a big change on its own.

> I am not sure this is good in general as does not make it obvious if that is millis or nanos nor if it is cached or raw.

Yeah I try and include that in the variable name. That's all we can do really when working with a bare `long` (which is most of the time) and I wouldn't want to introduce boxing just to encode this in the type system.

Thank you for your input! I changed thread pool in favor of LongSupplier. In ClusterModule it is bound to ThreadPool#relativeTimeInNanos whereas in tests - to System::nanoTime.

Regarding number of affected files. 
I deliberately did not introduce a new CTOR for AllocationService in order to set default value (read it 'hide') for LongSupplier param and hence leave existing AllocationService's referees (see them in tests) untouched. I think that newly introduced LongSupplier is important part of code contract and it should stay there until resolution of #95800

timeline.body: Thanks @volodk85; I left a couple of suggestions that I think will simplify this.

reply.body: You're correct. Please see full explanation in a the comment below

timeline.body: It looks suspicious that deterministic task queue might rely on a time supplied from outside (what if it gets out of sync with relativeTimeInMillis?). Is it possible to always rely on `TimeValue.timeValueMillis(currentTimeMillis).nanos()`?

reply.body:
Unfortunately it is not possible until #95800 is resolved.

If we were rely only on `TimeValue.timeValueMillis(currentTimeMillis).nanos()` there is a test SnapshotResiliencyTests#testSnapshotPrimaryRelocations which would become flaky.  In short, the test creates cluster with random number of master nodes and it works as expected iff there is only one master node is present. In case of multiple master nodes, the test simulates failure of master node to trigger new node election https://github.com/elastic/elasticsearch/blob/be78530dd28515634d57640d652a0a988e55cd17/server/src/test/java/org/elasticsearch/snapshots/SnapshotResiliencyTests.java#L1011-L1013
This is done to test snapshot creating during master node failure.

When cluster state changes and unassigned info flows via the wire. Upon receiving UnassignedInfo object gets created via its constructor with *unassignedTimeNanos* field set to current nano time
https://github.com/elastic/elasticsearch/blob/51e1188304fec338d4472b4e7a57c57356dbbdbf/server/src/main/java/org/elasticsearch/cluster/routing/UnassignedInfo.java#L298

Ultimately the test fails during *reroute* phase with assertion `assert nanoTimeNow >= unassignedTimeNanos` where *nanoTimeNow* comes from Deterministic task queue (and is artificial number which is not related to actual time flow) and *unassignedTimeNanos* is an actual nano time which is taken UnassignedInfo instance creation.

Bottom line 1
By providing *nanoTimeSupplier* in Deterministic task queue we are making *nanoTimeNow* and *unassignedTimeNanos* (from code above) mutually comparable since both of them are related to natural time flow for particular scenario.

Bottom line 2
Crux of #95800 is to stop relying on nano time for *RemainingDelay* calculation - the only one place where nano time is used in UnassignedInfo. When #95800 is fixed, we could remove *nanoTimeSupplier* from DeterministicTaskQueue and make code more cleaner.
